 LETTER: The student loan conundrum
 Cut interest rates to attack default levels.
 (Getty Images) More Stories LETTER: Tick tock LETTER: What does the AI future look like? LETTER: Democrats and ‘affordability’ LETTER: Both parties play dirty 
 Christopher Owen Las Vegas 
 November 3, 2026 - 9:01 pm 
 In response to the Review-Journal’s Oct. 26 editorial about colleges lowering tuition as student loan limits kick in:
 Sadly, the one thing that the Big Beautiful Bill didn’t do was deal with the existing studetn loan deficit of $1.9 trillion and counting. I have suggested many times that to significantly lower that amount requires only for Congress to retroactively lower the interest rate charged on student loans to 1 percent (to cover the cost of handling) from the current 3.1 percent to 8.1 percent. This would immediately reduce the student loan deficit and everybody’s obligation.
 It would also reduce the amount of loans being written off and likely increase the numbers of loans that are paid back.
 Doing this would not result in losses for the government. It would instead be a reduction of expected income, like a bank choosing to lower an individual’s mortgage rate. The bank still earns money, just not as much as it was going to. Why is Congress charging students so much interest that it creates this huge deficit? Shouldn’t the intent of government student loans be to help students?
 This should be a bipartisan effort as it has something for both Democrats and Republicans — the easing of student loan debt and a reduction of the student loan deficit. But, sadly, there has been virtually zero response from our federal politicians.
